title: Why consulting slides formatting takes hours for consultants on Mac, and how to fix it
metaTitle: Consulting slides formatting takes hours: fix it on Mac
description: Consulting slides formatting takes hours because brand rules live in people's heads. Here is how to fix it in PowerPoint on Mac.
intro: Consulting slides formatting takes hours because most decks get fixed by hand, one box at a time. The brand rules exist, but they live in a PDF, a partner's memory and a template nobody updated. The fix is to put the rules inside the file. This page shows how to do that on a Mac for free, and where a voice assistant like Lazur helps.
tldr: Most formatting time goes to fixing copied slides, not writing new ones.
Put brand rules inside the file: theme colors, theme fonts and one clean Slide Master.
Audit one live deck before you change anything, so you know if the problem is the master or the slides.
The cost figures are rough. Use your own hours and your own rate before you decide.
Lazur points, explains and guides. It does not format slides for you.

blocks.text: A consulting deck rarely starts from a blank file. You copy last month's deck, paste in new charts and pull slides from older projects. Each slide brings its own fonts, colors and spacing. Then someone has to pull all of it back into line with the brand guide. That pull back is where the hours go.
Where the hours actually go

Most people guess the time goes into writing. In practice, a lot of it goes into the fixing pass. You nudge a title a little to the left, match a gray that is almost right and reset a bullet indent someone set by hand. Each fix is small. Together they fill an afternoon.

items: Re-typing brand colors because the exact values were never saved in the file
Matching fonts on slides pasted in from an older template
Moving logos and footers that drifted off their usual spot
Fixing bullet indents and spacing one paragraph at a time
Rebuilding charts so the palette matches the brand guide
Checking the whole deck again after a reviewer changes one slide

blocks.text: What the hours cost in money

Start with the one figure that touches formatting time. It comes from a vendor blog, Imagine Layout, which cites a GfK survey for Made in Office. The blog says employees spend about 20 hours a month in PowerPoint, and roughly 8 of those on formatting. It does not link the original survey or give its year. Treat it as a rough signal, not a measured fact about consultants.

If you want a money number, you need a rate. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a median of $48.97 an hour for management analysts in its May 2025 data. Consultants may earn more or less, so swap in your own rate. Analyst pay is a proxy, not a consultant benchmark.

blocks.text: Multiply that by every person on the team, and the number grows quickly. Use it as a planning figure, not a payroll figure. Then test it. Track your own formatting time for a few weeks and compare the result with the table.
What the research says about slide design

The best study on this topic dates from 2013. Garner and Alley gave 110 engineering students slides built in one of two ways. One used assertion-evidence design. The other used PowerPoint default design. The assertion-evidence group had better comprehension, fewer misconceptions, lower perceived cognitive load and better delayed recall.

Be careful with what this proves. The study compared two design styles. It did not test off-brand fonts or colors, and it did not measure time spent fixing slides. The abstract gives no effect sizes, so do not quote one. Use it to justify clean, consistent design, not to promise a specific result.
Run a brand audit before you touch a slide

A short audit shows whether the problem sits in one deck or in the master. Run it on a deck that is nearly final. Do not start on a blank slide. Write down what you find, because the list becomes your fix list.

items: Open the brand guide and copy the exact color values and font names into one note.
Go to Design > Variants > Colors and check whether your brand colors are already in the list.
Go to View > Slide Master and note which fonts the master uses for titles and body text.
Scroll the deck and tag every slide that breaks a rule. Use one tag per problem, such as font, color or position.
Count the tags by type. A pile of font tags points at the master. Scattered tags point at the slides.
Save the audit next to the deck, so reviewers check the same list.

blocks.title: Fix the master first
blocks.text: Fix the master before you fix slides. If you correct slides one by one while the master is still wrong, you will redo the work after the master changes. Keep an untouched copy of the deck so you can compare the before and after.
Mistakes that make slide formatting worse

items: Pasting slides from another client deck without checking the master first.
Using free text boxes for titles when the layout already has placeholders.
Changing the font on one slide only, then calling the deck done.
Letting every reviewer edit the master at the same time, with no owner.
Trusting an old template because it looks close enough at a glance.
Skipping the final pass because the meeting is close.

blocks.text: How Microsoft's brand tools fit in

Microsoft offers two routes. Theme colors and theme fonts live inside the file, so they cost nothing extra. Brand Kit is a Microsoft 365 Copilot feature. A brand owner uploads a template. When strict brand adherence is On, Copilot uses only that template and its slide master layouts.

Brand Kit has limits. Microsoft says Copilot does not change font or placeholder sizes. It may add design elements to fit extra content. Only the Brand Kit owner or a brand manager can change its settings, and end users cannot override them. Templates must be made in PowerPoint for Windows or Mac, not the web.

blocks.title: Check the license first
blocks.text: The sources behind this page did not confirm Brand Kit pricing, because Microsoft's price pages would not load. Ask your IT team whether your firm's plan includes Copilot before you plan around Brand Kit.

Microsoft also advises varied sample slides and text placeholders, rather than text boxes. Without enough sample slides, Copilot falls back to the Slide Master, which may give less optimal results. The same advice helps when you work by hand.
Where Lazur fits in

Lazur does not fix your formatting. It points at controls on your screen, explains what they do and guides you one click at a time. It also dictates text and drafts notes. That helps when you learn Microsoft's menus or walk a colleague through a fix. Every change still comes from your hand.

Here is a typical session. Open the deck and hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask where Customize Colors sits. Lazur circles it. You make the click, then ask what the next setting does. Lazur answers out loud while you work. For the wider setup, see [PowerPoint for consultants on Mac](/for/consultants/powerpoint).
Client data and your firm's rules

Slides often hold client names, figures and draft strategy. Before you paste any of it into an AI tool, check your firm's rules on client data. If your firm limits AI tools for client work, do the fixes by hand. Theme colors, theme fonts and the master need no outside service.
Next steps for a repeatable deck

If rebuilding old decks keeps eating your time, read [how to stop rebuilding past consulting work from scratch](/for/consultants/problems/rebuilding-past-consulting-work-scratch). If a deck has the wrong page shape, check [how to change slide size in PowerPoint on Mac](/how-to/change-slide-size-in-powerpoint). Both steps help the master do its job.

faq.question: Why does consulting slides formatting take so long?
faq.answer: Most of the time goes to fixing copied slides by hand. Each copy carries old fonts, colors and spacing. Fixing them one at a time is slow, and reviewers often add more changes. Fix the theme and the master first, and much of that work stops.

faq.question: Is the 8 hours a month figure reliable?
faq.answer: Not yet. It comes from a vendor blog that cites a GfK survey for Made in Office. The blog gives no survey year and no link to the original study. Use it as a rough sign, then track your own time for a few weeks.

faq.question: Where do I set brand colors in PowerPoint for Mac?
faq.answer: Go to Design > Variants > Colors > Customize Colors. Pick your colors in Create New Theme Colors, name the set and choose Save. The set has 12 slots, including six accent colors and two hyperlink colors.

faq.question: Can Lazur format my slides?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or edit files for you. It points at controls on your screen, explains them out loud and guides you one click at a time. You make the changes yourself.

faq.question: Do I need Microsoft 365 Copilot to fix this?
faq.answer: No. Theme colors and theme fonts work without it. Brand Kit is a Copilot feature. Check with your IT team about your plan, because the sources for this page did not confirm Brand Kit pricing.

faq.question: Can I put client slides into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Check your firm's rules on client data first. If your firm restricts AI tools, do the fixes by hand. Theme colors, theme fonts and the Slide Master need no outside service.

faq.question: Does Keynote have the same theme options?
faq.answer: Keynote for Mac can save a custom theme with File > Save Theme. Apple's page says only changes to slide layouts are saved to a new theme. Check colors and fonts yourself on a test deck before you rely on it.

faq.question: What is the first step if I have very little time?
faq.answer: Set the theme colors. Go to Design > Variants > Colors > Customize Colors. Then check the title and body fonts in View > Slide Master. Those two changes help every new slide you build.

problem: slide formatting that breaks brand rules

costs.title: Hours you lose every month
costs.text: A vendor blog cites about 8 hours a month on formatting, out of about 20 hours in PowerPoint. The source is unverified, so use it as a rough sign. If it is anywhere near right, formatting eats a real share of your week. Track your own hours for a couple of weeks.

costs.title: Money at a proxy rate
costs.text: At the BLS median of $48.97 an hour, 8 hours a month comes to about $4,700 a year per person. That is my arithmetic, using analyst pay as a stand-in for consultant pay. Plug in your own rate. The number moves with it.

costs.title: Rework after review
costs.text: Every review round can send a slide back to the formatting queue. A reviewer changes one box, and the fix spreads to other slides that copied it. No study I found measures this rework, so treat it as a pattern to watch, not a number to quote.

costs.title: Off-brand decks you cannot measure
costs.text: Inconsistent formatting can make a deck look careless to a client. I found no study that measures this effect on consultants or their clients. Do not promise a result you cannot show. Use consistency as a quality check, not a sales claim.

costs.title: Team time nobody tracks
costs.text: Formatting work often sits outside project budgets. Nobody bills it, so it looks free. It still uses hours that could go to analysis, client calls or writing. Name the cost in your next team meeting, even if you cannot price it exactly.

causes.title: Copied slides carry their own formatting
causes.text: Most consulting decks are built by copying older decks. Each copied slide brings its fonts, colors and spacing with it. Those values drift a little each time. After a few copies, nobody can say which version is the real one.

causes.title: The brand rules live outside the file
causes.text: The brand guide is often a PDF or a slide nobody opens. The file itself may still hold default theme colors and fonts. When the rules are not in the master, every person guesses. The guesses differ, and the deck shows it.

causes.title: Text boxes replace placeholders
causes.text: A free text box has no link to the layout. Change the layout later, and the box stays where it is. Microsoft advises placeholders over text boxes when working with its Copilot templates. The same logic helps manual work, because placeholders keep the master's fonts and positions.

causes.title: Nobody owns the master
causes.text: In many teams, anyone can edit the master, so nobody does. Microsoft's Brand Kit model gives control to the owner or a brand manager, and end users cannot override those settings. Your team can copy that idea with a named owner, even without the license.

causes.title: Review rounds scatter small fixes
causes.text: Reviewers change a title, a color or a note on the slide itself. They rarely fix the layout behind it. Each small change stays local, and the next copy brings the old version back into the deck.

causes.title: Deadlines push cleanup to the end
causes.text: Formatting is often the last task before a meeting, so it gets the least time. Errors survive because nobody checks the whole deck after the final edit. The fastest fix is a short check that runs every time, not a heroic pass at night.

causes.title: Learning the menus takes longer than it should
causes.text: Theme settings sit in menus people rarely open. Many consultants learned PowerPoint by copying old slides, not by building masters. Without a walkthrough, the easy path is copying, and the copying repeats the problem.

fixes.title: Set your theme colors once
fixes.text: Go to Design > Variants > Colors > Customize Colors. Pick your brand colors in Create New Theme Colors, name the set and choose Save. A theme color set has 12 slots: four text and background colors, six accent colors and two hyperlink colors. Fill them all, so charts and new shapes pick up brand values.

fixes.title: Set theme fonts in the Slide Master
fixes.text: Go to View > Slide Master. On the Slide Master tab, select Fonts > Customize Fonts. Choose heading and body fonts in Create New Theme Fonts, then Save. Microsoft's written font steps are mostly for Windows, and its macOS section covers colors in less detail. If Customize Fonts is missing on your Mac, set the title and body fonts on the master slides, then check a sample slide.

fixes.title: Clean up one master, then copy it
fixes.text: Keep one master file for each brand. Fix the title, body, chart and section layouts there. Build new decks from that file, not from last quarter's deck. When a project starts, copy the master, not the content.

fixes.title: Replace text boxes with placeholders
fixes.text: Where a layout has a title or body placeholder, type into it. Avoid free-floating text boxes for headings. Microsoft recommends placeholders for its own Copilot templates. The same habit keeps fonts and positions consistent when you work by hand.

fixes.title: Write a one-page brand sheet
fixes.text: Put the exact color values, the two fonts, the logo rules and the margin rule on one page. Store it in the same folder as the master. Reviewers can then check a slide without opening the full brand guide.

fixes.title: If you use Keynote, check what carries over
fixes.text: Keynote for Mac can save a custom theme with File > Save Theme. Apple's page says only changes to slide layouts are saved to a new theme. It does not say colors or fonts carry over. Check those by hand, and test the saved theme on a new deck before you rely on it.

fixes.title: Use Brand Kit if your firm already pays for Copilot
fixes.text: This route costs money, so skip it if you want a free fix. If your firm already has Microsoft 365 Copilot, ask a brand manager to upload a template with Create > More > Brand kits > open kit > Templates > Add to Brand kit. Set strict brand adherence to On for the tightest control. Templates must be built in PowerPoint for Windows or Mac, not the web.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pull the rules into one place
plan.text: Copy the exact colors and fonts from your brand guide into one page. Add the logo rules and the margin rules. Keep the page in the same folder as the master file, so reviewers find it.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Audit one live deck
plan.text: Run the audit list on a deck that is nearly final. Tag each broken slide by problem type. Count the tags by type, not by slide, so the pattern shows.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set theme colors and fonts
plan.text: Set the theme colors through Design > Variants > Colors > Customize Colors. Then set the theme fonts from View > Slide Master, or check the options your Mac build shows. Save each set with a clear name.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Rebuild the layouts
plan.text: Fix the title, body, chart and section layouts in the master. Replace text boxes with placeholders on the sample slides. Then test a new slide from the master. If the text looks wrong, fix the master, not the slide.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Pilot and lock the routine
plan.text: Build one short deck from the master and ask a colleague to review it. Note which slides still need hand fixes. Save the master in a shared folder with one named owner. Schedule a short check each month.
